question: Acute kidney disease is classified by the location or mechanism producing reduced kidney function. Which category is defined by reduced renal perfusion?
cited_learning_objective: Establish a differential diagnosis for acute kidney disease (AKD)

options.rationale: Pre-renal disease results from reduced kidney perfusion caused by low extracellular fluid volume or altered renal hemodynamics.
Glomerular disease is an intra-renal process; glomerular inflammation or injury would make this category correct.
Tubulointerstitial disease is an intra-renal process; tubular or interstitial injury would make this category correct.
Post-renal disease results from interference with urine flow; urinary tract obstruction would make this category correct.
Renal vascular disease is classified as intra-renal; direct medium- or small-vessel injury would make this category correct.

question: Urine microscopy is performed in a patient with suspected ischemic tubular injury. Which sediment finding most strongly supports this diagnosis?
cited_learning_objective: Recognize urine findings in prerenal AKD and acute tubular necrosis (ATN)

options.rationale: Hyaline casts support a pre-renal process; concentrated urine with preserved tubular function would make this finding appropriate.
Pigmented granular muddy brown casts reflect renal tubular epithelial injury and support acute tubular necrosis.
Red blood cell casts support glomerulonephritis; glomerular bleeding and inflammation would make this finding appropriate.
White blood cell casts support interstitial nephritis or pyelonephritis; interstitial inflammation would make this finding appropriate.
Urinary eosinophils can accompany interstitial nephritis or atheroemboli; either corresponding disorder would make this finding appropriate.

question: Which fractional excretion of urea result supports a pre-renal process?
cited_learning_objective: Recognize urine findings in prerenal AKD and acute tubular necrosis (ATN)

options.rationale: A value above 70% is not the pre-renal pattern; marked tubular dysfunction consistent with acute tubular necrosis would support this result.
A value above 50% suggests acute tubular necrosis; tubular injury would make this result appropriate.
A value of 50% does not meet the stated pre-renal threshold; a value at or below 35% would support preserved urea reabsorption.
A fractional excretion of urea at or below 35% supports a pre-renal process.
A value above 35% exceeds the stated pre-renal threshold; a value above 50% would instead support acute tubular necrosis.

question: Which microscopic finding is most characteristic of medication-induced interstitial kidney inflammation?
cited_learning_objective: Recognize acute interstitial nephritis (AIN) as a cause of AKD

options.rationale: Tubular necrosis supports acute tubular necrosis; injured tubules with granular casts would make this finding appropriate.
A primary glomerular lesion does not match acute interstitial nephritis; glomerulonephritis would make this pattern appropriate.
Vascular thrombi support a thrombotic microangiopathy; small-vessel injury would make this pattern appropriate.
Tubular crystals support obstructive crystal injury; intratubular crystal deposition would make this pattern appropriate.

options.text: Interstitial inflammatory infiltrate with normal glomeruli
options.rationale: Acute interstitial nephritis produces an inflammatory interstitial infiltrate while the glomeruli remain normal.

question: A urine sample has a specific gravity of 1.010 and pigmented granular casts. Which process best integrates these findings?
cited_learning_objective: Recognize urine findings in prerenal AKD and acute tubular necrosis (ATN)

options.rationale: Acute tubular necrosis impairs tubular concentrating function and produces pigmented granular casts.
Pre-renal volume depletion should preserve concentrating ability and produce hyaline casts; those findings would make this diagnosis correct.
Glomerular inflammation is associated with red blood cells, red blood cell casts, and proteinuria; those findings would support this diagnosis.
Interstitial nephritis is associated with white blood cells, white blood cell casts, or eosinophils; those findings would support this diagnosis.
Post-renal disease requires interference with urine flow; collecting-system dilation or bladder obstruction would support this diagnosis.

question: A patient taking a diuretic has acute kidney dysfunction, and sodium-based urine indices may be misleading. Which result most directly supports reduced kidney perfusion?
cited_learning_objective: Recognize urine findings in prerenal AKD and acute tubular necrosis (ATN)

options.rationale: Urine sodium above 30 supports acute tubular necrosis but can also occur after diuretic use; tubular injury without recent diuretics would make it more diagnostic.
Fractional urea excretion of 30% is at or below 35% and supports a pre-renal process despite recent diuretic exposure.
Fractional sodium excretion above 2% usually supports acute tubular necrosis but may be elevated by recent diuretic use.
Urine osmolality below 500 reflects impaired concentration and supports tubular injury; a value above 500 would support reduced perfusion.
Specific gravity near 1.010 supports impaired tubular concentration; a value above 1.020 would support a pre-renal process.

question: Reduced kidney perfusion persists long enough to cause structural tubular injury. Which sequence best describes the relationship between these processes?
cited_learning_objective: Establish a differential diagnosis for acute kidney disease (AKD)

options.rationale: Obstruction produces post-renal disease rather than the stated transition; collecting-system interference followed by renal injury would support this sequence.

options.text: Interstitial inflammation followed by volume depletion
options.rationale: Interstitial inflammation is an intra-renal process and is not the stated consequence of prolonged hypoperfusion; medication exposure with inflammatory urine would support it.

options.text: Pre-renal disease followed by ischemic ATN
options.rationale: A prolonged pre-renal state can progress from functional hypoperfusion to ischemic acute tubular necrosis.

options.text: Glomerular disease followed by urinary obstruction
options.rationale: Glomerular disease and urinary obstruction are separate intra-renal and post-renal processes; evidence of both sequential lesions would be required.

options.text: Vascular disease followed by crystal obstruction
options.rationale: Vascular injury does not produce the described hypoperfusion-to-tubular-injury sequence; vascular findings followed by deposited crystals would support this sequence.

question: A patient has red blood cells, red blood cell casts, and proteinuria on urine microscopy. Which intra-renal category is most strongly supported?
cited_learning_objective: Recognize urine findings in other causes of AKD besides prerenal AKD and ATN

options.rationale: Acute tubular injury produces renal tubular epithelial cells and pigmented casts; those findings would support this category.
Interstitial inflammation produces white blood cells, white blood cell casts, or eosinophils; those findings would support this category.
Tubular obstruction is associated with intratubular crystals or casts; identification of those obstructing materials would support this category.
Red blood cells, red blood cell casts, and proteinuria form the urine pattern of glomerular injury.
Pre-renal disease usually has normal sediment or hyaline casts; a bland concentrated urine would support this category.

question: A patient develops a creatinine increase after iodinated contrast exposure. Which paired findings most strongly distinguish tubular injury from persistent volume depletion?
cited_learning_objective: Recognize urine findings in prerenal AKD and acute tubular necrosis (ATN)

options.rationale: Hyaline casts and concentrated urine indicate preserved tubular function during a pre-renal process.

options.text: Low urine sodium and concentrated urine
options.rationale: Low urine sodium and concentrated urine support renal sodium and water conservation during reduced perfusion.

options.text: Low sodium excretion and hyaline casts
options.rationale: Low fractional sodium excretion with hyaline casts favors pre-renal disease, although contrast injury can sometimes have low sodium excretion.

options.text: High urine osmolality and low sodium
options.rationale: High urine osmolality with low urine sodium supports intact tubular conservation in a pre-renal state.
Granular casts with specific gravity near 1.010 demonstrate tubular injury and loss of concentrating capacity.

question: Which combination correctly matches an acute tubular necrosis phase with its defining feature?
cited_learning_objective: Establish a differential diagnosis for acute kidney disease (AKD)

options.text: Initiating phase with evolving tubular injury
options.rationale: The initiating phase lasts hours to a day from the precipitating event until tubular injury occurs.
The maintenance phase has markedly decreased glomerular filtration; normalized filtration would instead occur with recovery.

options.text: Recovery phase with progressive electrolyte risk
options.rationale: The recovery phase involves tissue repair and falling blood urea nitrogen and creatinine; marked electrolyte risk characterizes maintenance.

options.text: Initiating phase with complete tissue repair
options.rationale: Complete tissue repair belongs to recovery; a recent precipitating event with evolving injury would indicate initiation.

options.text: Maintenance phase with baseline creatinine restoration
options.rationale: Baseline creatinine restoration occurs during recovery; persistent low filtration over 1-3 weeks characterizes maintenance.

question: A low fractional excretion of sodium is measured in a patient with acute kidney dysfunction. Which condition can produce this result despite established tubular injury?
cited_learning_objective: Recognize urine findings in prerenal AKD and acute tubular necrosis (ATN)

options.rationale: Recent diuretic use tends to increase sodium excretion; a fractional sodium excretion above 2% would fit that setting.
Radiocontrast-associated acute tubular necrosis may retain a fractional sodium excretion below 1%.
Chronic kidney disease can produce fractional sodium excretion above 2%; chronic dysfunction with that elevated value would support this option.
Diuretic-associated sodium wasting elevates fractional sodium excretion; recent diuretic exposure with a value above 2% would support it.
Established acute tubular necrosis generally produces fractional sodium excretion above 2%; that elevated result would support this option.

question: Which combination most strongly supports a post-renal cause of acute kidney dysfunction?
cited_learning_objective: Establish a differential diagnosis for acute kidney disease (AKD)

options.rationale: Flat neck veins and hypotension support reduced circulating volume; a concentrated urine response would further support pre-renal disease.
Granular casts with isosthenuria support acute tubular necrosis; nephrotoxic or ischemic exposure would strengthen that diagnosis.
Inflammatory casts with normal glomeruli support interstitial nephritis; medication exposure and interstitial infiltrates would strengthen that diagnosis.
Collecting-system dilation and retained urine indicate interference with urinary flow, defining a post-renal process.
Red blood cell casts and proteinuria support glomerular disease; glomerular inflammation would make this combination appropriate.

question: A patient has white blood cells and white blood cell casts without evidence of collecting-system obstruction. Which renal compartment is most likely injured?
cited_learning_objective: Recognize urine findings in other causes of AKD besides prerenal AKD and ATN

options.rationale: White blood cells and white blood cell casts localize inflammation to the tubulointerstitial compartment.
Glomerular capillary injury produces hematuria, red blood cell casts, and proteinuria; those findings would support this compartment.
Medium-vessel disorders are vascular causes of intra-renal disease; evidence of polyarteritis nodosa or Kawasaki disease would support this compartment.
Collecting-system injury would require structural or functional interference with urine flow; dilation or retention would support this compartment.
A glomerular lesion would produce red blood cell casts and proteinuria rather than the stated inflammatory sediment.

question: Which paired urine findings indicate preserved tubular conservation during reduced effective renal perfusion?
cited_learning_objective: Recognize urine findings in prerenal AKD and acute tubular necrosis (ATN)

options.rationale: Specific gravity near 1.010 with granular casts indicates impaired concentration from tubular injury.
Urine sodium above 30 with isosthenuria supports acute tubular necrosis rather than preserved conservation.

options.text: Urea excretion above 50% and granular casts
options.rationale: Fractional urea excretion above 50% with granular casts supports acute tubular necrosis.

options.text: Sodium excretion above 2% and dilute urine
options.rationale: Fractional sodium excretion above 2% with dilute urine indicates impaired tubular sodium and water retention.

options.text: Urine osmolality above 500 and hyaline casts
options.rationale: High urine osmolality with hyaline casts reflects preserved concentrating function during a pre-renal process.

question: A medication causes loss of an intrarenal mediator that normally supports filtration during poor perfusion. Which arteriolar change explains the resulting decrease in glomerular filtration?
cited_learning_objective: Establish a differential diagnosis for acute kidney disease (AKD)

options.rationale: Efferent constriction helps maintain glomerular pressure during reduced perfusion; preserved filtration would make this response appropriate.
Reduced afferent constriction would increase inflow rather than explain the filtration decrease; enhanced afferent dilation would support maintenance.
Nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs block intrarenal prostaglandins and attenuate compensatory afferent dilation.
Reduced efferent dilation implies greater efferent constriction, which supports glomerular pressure rather than causing the described decrease.
Increased afferent dilation is the compensatory response that maintains filtration during reduced perfusion.

question: A 75-year-old man has declining urine output several hours after surgery. Blood pressure is 100/60 mm Hg, pulse is 100/min, and neck veins are not visible. Serum creatinine is 1.5 mg/dL [0.8-1.2 mg/dL], increased from 0.9 mg/dL on admission. Which diagnosis best explains the acute change?
cited_learning_objective: Establish a differential diagnosis for acute kidney disease (AKD)

options.rationale: Chronic kidney disease requires dysfunction for at least 3 months or chronic structural changes; a sustained baseline reduction or small echogenic kidneys would support it.
Post-renal disease requires impaired urinary flow; retention or collecting-system dilation would support this diagnosis.
Glomerular disease requires findings such as red blood cell casts and proteinuria; those findings would support this diagnosis.
The rapid creatinine rise from a recent baseline with falling urine output establishes acute kidney injury.
Acute interstitial nephritis would be supported by white blood cells, white blood cell casts, eosinophils, or an inflammatory interstitial infiltrate.

question: A 75-year-old man develops oliguria after surgery while taking hydrochlorothiazide and receiving ketorolac. He has flat neck veins and relative hypotension. Urine contains hyaline casts, urine sodium is 15, and fractional sodium excretion is 0.1%. Which process is most likely?
cited_learning_objective: Recognize urine findings in prerenal AKD and acute tubular necrosis (ATN)

options.rationale: Volume depletion, bland sediment, low urine sodium, and fractional sodium excretion below 1% support a pre-renal process.
Contrast-associated injury requires iodinated contrast exposure and usually granular casts; that exposure and sediment would support this diagnosis.
Interstitial nephritis requires inflammatory urine findings such as white blood cells or white blood cell casts; those findings would support this diagnosis.
Glomerular inflammation produces red blood cells, red blood cell casts, and proteinuria; that sediment would support this diagnosis.
Post-renal injury requires obstruction or retained urine; collecting-system dilation or bladder retention would support this diagnosis.

question: A postoperative patient with flat neck veins, blood pressure of 100/60 mm Hg, and urine output of 8 mL/hr has no collecting-system dilation. Urine microscopy shows hyaline casts. Which next management step is most appropriate?
cited_learning_objective: Establish a differential diagnosis for acute kidney disease (AKD)

options.rationale: Continuing the diuretic would worsen volume depletion; volume excess with elevated venous pressure would be required for this strategy.
Normal saline restores perfusion, while discontinuing hydrochlorothiazide removes a contributor to extracellular fluid volume loss.
Saline addresses depletion, but ketorolac can further lower filtration by blocking compensatory prostaglandins and should not be continued.
No infection-related kidney process is demonstrated; fever, inflammatory sediment, or an infection source would support antibiotics.
Steroids may accelerate recovery in interstitial nephritis; biopsy-supported interstitial inflammation would make this approach appropriate.

question: A volume-depleted postoperative patient receives ketorolac and develops worsening oliguria. Which mechanism most directly accounts for the medication-related reduction in filtration?
cited_learning_objective: Establish a differential diagnosis for acute kidney disease (AKD)

options.rationale: Enhanced afferent dilation would preserve glomerular filtration; an intact compensatory response would produce this effect.
The described prostaglandin effect occurs at the afferent arteriole; loss of efferent constriction is not the stated ketorolac mechanism.
Prostaglandins are vasodilatory in this setting rather than constrictive; a different mediator causing afferent constriction would be required.
Efferent dilation would not explain preservation of filtration during poor perfusion and is not the stated effect of ketorolac.
Ketorolac blocks intrarenal vasodilatory prostaglandins, attenuating afferent dilation and reducing glomerular filtration.

question: A postoperative patient with oliguria receives normal saline, and hydrochlorothiazide is discontinued. Blood pressure rises from 100/60 to 125/80 mm Hg, and urine output increases from 8 to 45 mL/hr. Which diagnosis is best supported by this response?
cited_learning_objective: Establish a differential diagnosis for acute kidney disease (AKD)

options.rationale: Rapid improvement in blood pressure and urine output after volume replacement supports reversible perfusion-dependent kidney dysfunction.
Established tubular necrosis would not be expected to reverse immediately with saline; granular casts and persistent dysfunction would support it.
Interstitial nephritis improves after withdrawal of the offending drug and may require steroids; inflammatory urine or biopsy findings would support it.
Glomerular disease would produce hematuria, proteinuria, and red blood cell casts rather than rapid volume responsiveness.
Obstruction improves after relief of impaired urine flow; retained urine or collecting-system dilation would support this diagnosis.

question: A 55-year-old man with baseline creatinine of 1.4 mg/dL undergoes contrast-enhanced abdominal imaging. Twenty-four hours later, creatinine is 2.0 mg/dL despite intravenous fluids. Ultrasound shows no hydronephrosis, and urine specific gravity is 1.010 with pigmented granular casts. Which diagnosis is most likely?
cited_learning_objective: Recognize urine findings in prerenal AKD and acute tubular necrosis (ATN)

options.rationale: Pre-renal disease should produce concentrated urine and hyaline casts; those findings with volume responsiveness would support it.
The 24-hour creatinine rise after iodinated contrast, isosthenuria, and granular casts support nephrotoxic acute tubular necrosis.
Interstitial nephritis would produce white blood cells, white blood cell casts, and an interstitial infiltrate; those findings would support it.
Glomerulonephritis produces red blood cells, red blood cell casts, and proteinuria; that active sediment would support it.
Post-renal injury requires impaired urine flow; hydronephrosis, bladder retention, or catheter-responsive output would support it.

question: A patient develops acute tubular injury after iodinated contrast administration. Kidney ultrasound excludes obstruction, and perfusion has been optimized. Which management strategy is most appropriate?
cited_learning_objective: Establish a differential diagnosis for acute kidney disease (AKD)

options.rationale: Diuretics and nephrotoxins may add renal insults; volume excess with a separate indication would be needed before considering diuresis.
Reduced perfusion and additional contrast can worsen tubular injury; neither is appropriate during recovery.
Management of contrast-associated tubular necrosis includes avoiding additional nephrotoxic agents and preventing further pre-renal or ischemic insults.
Steroids may speed recovery from interstitial nephritis; biopsy-supported interstitial inflammation would make steroid therapy appropriate.
Antibiotic withdrawal is appropriate when a drug causes interstitial nephritis, while limiting kidney perfusion would be harmful here.

question: A patient with contrast-associated tubular injury has creatinine values of 2.0 mg/dL on hospital days 2-4 after a baseline of 1.4 mg/dL. Which phase is most consistent with this plateau and continued risk of electrolyte abnormalities?
cited_learning_objective: Establish a differential diagnosis for acute kidney disease (AKD)

options.rationale: The initiating phase covers the hours to a day between the precipitating event and established tubular injury.
Pre-renal disease is a cause rather than a phase of acute tubular necrosis; reversible hypoperfusion without established injury would support it.
Obstruction is a post-renal mechanism rather than an acute tubular necrosis phase; impaired urine flow would support it.
The maintenance phase features markedly reduced filtration and risk of electrolyte abnormalities over approximately 1-3 weeks.
The recovery phase involves tissue repair and return of blood urea nitrogen and creatinine toward baseline.

question: A patient recovers from contrast-associated tubular injury, with creatinine returning from 2.0 to 1.4 mg/dL. Two days later, while taking ciprofloxacin, creatinine increases to 4.0 mg/dL. Urine contains white blood cells and white blood cell casts. Which diagnosis best explains the new injury?
cited_learning_objective: Recognize acute interstitial nephritis (AIN) as a cause of AKD

options.rationale: Contrast-associated tubular necrosis would follow contrast exposure and produce granular casts; renewed contrast exposure with that sediment would support it.
Pre-renal injury should produce concentrated urine and hyaline casts; volume depletion with those findings would support it.
The delayed creatinine rise during ciprofloxacin therapy with white blood cells and white blood cell casts supports drug-induced interstitial nephritis.
Post-renal injury requires impaired urine flow; hydronephrosis or bladder retention would support it.
Glomerulonephritis would produce red blood cell casts and proteinuria; that sediment would support this diagnosis.

question: A patient taking ciprofloxacin develops creatinine of 4.0 mg/dL [0.8-1.2 mg/dL]. Urine microscopy shows white blood cell casts, and biopsy shows interstitial inflammatory cells with normal glomeruli. Which next management step is most appropriate?
cited_learning_objective: Recognize acute interstitial nephritis (AIN) as a cause of AKD

options.rationale: Continuing the causative medication sustains interstitial inflammation; saline alone is appropriate for volume-responsive pre-renal disease.
Ketorolac can impair filtration, and continuing ciprofloxacin preserves the suspected trigger; neither addresses the interstitial injury.
Additional contrast introduces another nephrotoxic insult; contrast imaging would require a separate compelling indication.
Withdrawal of the offending drug is the central management step, and renal function usually returns toward the premorbid state.
A diuretic does not remove the inflammatory trigger, and continued ciprofloxacin may perpetuate the injury.

question: A patient with biopsy-supported medication-induced interstitial nephritis has the suspected drug discontinued. Kidney function remains impaired during early follow-up. Which additional intervention may accelerate recovery?
cited_learning_objective: Recognize acute interstitial nephritis (AIN) as a cause of AKD

options.rationale: Restarting the offending drug can perpetuate interstitial inflammation; resolution after withdrawal would support continued avoidance.
Additional contrast can cause nephrotoxic tubular injury; a separate diagnostic necessity would be required for its use.
Nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs can reduce filtration by attenuating afferent dilation; they do not treat the interstitial infiltrate.
Diuretic-associated volume loss can add a pre-renal insult; clear volume excess would be required before resuming it.
Steroids may speed renal recovery after the offending medication has been removed.

question: A 55-year-old man has creatinine of 4.0 mg/dL [0.8-1.2 mg/dL], elevated neck veins, bibasilar rales, and ankle edema. Ultrasound shows no obstruction. Urine contains white blood cells and white blood cell casts after several days of antibiotic therapy. Which proposed mechanism best fits the findings?
cited_learning_objective: Recognize acute interstitial nephritis (AIN) as a cause of AKD

options.text: Reduced perfusion from extracellular volume depletion
options.rationale: The examination shows volume excess rather than depletion; flat neck veins, hypotension, and concentrated urine would support this mechanism.
Medication exposure followed by inflammatory urine sediment supports an intra-renal interstitial process.

options.text: Tubular necrosis from new contrast exposure
options.rationale: New contrast-associated injury would require recent contrast exposure and would produce pigmented granular casts.
Post-renal injury requires retained urine or collecting-system dilation; the negative ultrasound argues against this mechanism.
Glomerular inflammation would produce red blood cell casts and prominent proteinuria; those findings would support this mechanism.

question: A patient with acute kidney dysfunction has fractional sodium excretion below 1%, but microscopy reveals red blood cell casts and proteinuria. Which interpretation is most appropriate?
cited_learning_objective: Recognize urine findings in other causes of AKD besides prerenal AKD and ATN

options.rationale: Fractional sodium excretion below 1% is not specific for pre-renal disease; a bland sediment with hyaline casts would support that conclusion.

options.text: Acute tubular necrosis is definitively established
options.rationale: Acute tubular necrosis usually produces granular casts; that sediment with impaired concentrating indices would support it.
Glomerulonephritis or vasculitis can have fractional sodium excretion below 1%, while red blood cell casts and proteinuria localize injury to the glomerulus.
Post-renal disease requires evidence of impaired urine flow; hydronephrosis or urinary retention would support it.
Interstitial nephritis produces white blood cells, white blood cell casts, or eosinophils rather than red blood cell casts.

question: A hospitalized patient develops oliguria. Catheter placement leaves the bladder empty, and ultrasound shows normal-sized kidneys without collecting-system dilation. Which diagnostic category is least supported by these findings?
cited_learning_objective: Establish a differential diagnosis for acute kidney disease (AKD)

options.rationale: Normal imaging does not exclude pre-renal disease; hypotension, volume loss, and concentrated urine would support this category.
Normal imaging does not exclude tubular injury; granular casts and impaired concentrating ability would support this category.
Normal imaging does not exclude interstitial nephritis; inflammatory urine and an interstitial infiltrate would support this category.
Normal imaging does not exclude glomerular disease; red blood cell casts and proteinuria would support this category.
An empty bladder and absence of collecting-system dilation make obstructed urine flow the least supported category.

question: A patient with suspected acute kidney injury has recent diuretic exposure. Fractional sodium excretion is 2.5%, fractional urea excretion is 30%, and urine microscopy shows hyaline casts. Which diagnosis best integrates the findings?
cited_learning_objective: Recognize urine findings in prerenal AKD and acute tubular necrosis (ATN)

options.rationale: Recent diuretic use can elevate fractional sodium excretion, while fractional urea excretion at or below 35% and hyaline casts support a pre-renal process.
Acute tubular necrosis would be supported by granular casts and fractional urea excretion above 50%.
Interstitial nephritis would produce white blood cells, white blood cell casts, or eosinophils rather than hyaline casts.
Glomerular disease would produce red blood cells, red blood cell casts, and proteinuria rather than a bland sediment.
Post-renal injury requires evidence of impaired urine flow; hydronephrosis or bladder retention would support it.

question: A 55-year-old man has a creatinine increase 24 hours after iodinated contrast. Urine microscopy shows granular casts, but fractional sodium excretion is 0.8%. Which explanation best reconciles these results?
cited_learning_objective: Recognize urine findings in prerenal AKD and acute tubular necrosis (ATN)

options.text: The granular casts establish glomerular injury
options.rationale: Granular casts indicate tubular injury; red blood cell casts and proteinuria would establish glomerular disease.

options.text: The sodium result excludes tubular injury
options.rationale: A low fractional sodium excretion does not exclude radiocontrast-associated tubular necrosis.

options.text: The findings establish urinary tract obstruction
options.rationale: Urinary tract obstruction requires evidence of impaired urine flow; collecting-system dilation or bladder retention would support it.

options.text: Contrast injury may retain sodium avidity
options.rationale: Radiocontrast-associated acute tubular necrosis is a recognized exception in which fractional sodium excretion may remain below 1%.
Interstitial inflammation is supported by white blood cells, white blood cell casts, eosinophils, or an interstitial infiltrate.

question: A patient with acute tubular necrosis enters a period during which renal tissue repair occurs and blood urea nitrogen and creatinine return toward baseline. Which phase is occurring?
cited_learning_objective: Establish a differential diagnosis for acute kidney disease (AKD)

options.rationale: The initiating phase extends from the precipitating event until tubular injury develops; a recent insult with evolving injury would support it.
The maintenance phase features markedly reduced filtration and electrolyte risk; persistent dysfunction over 1-3 weeks would support it.
Pre-renal disease is an etiologic category rather than a phase of acute tubular necrosis; reversible hypoperfusion would support that process.
Post-renal disease is an etiologic category caused by impaired urine flow; obstruction would support that process.
The recovery phase is defined by renal tissue repair and return of blood urea nitrogen and creatinine toward normal.
